clinicalScope: Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) in adults and adolescents presenting in low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome
subject: Medicine
summary: AIDS is the late stage of HIV infection when the immune system is severely weakened, leading to life‑threatening infections and cancers. In East Africa it often presents with opportunistic diseases that are common locally and may be hard to diagnose without advanced tests.

sections.p: AIDS is defined by a CD4+ T‑cell count <200 cells/µL or the presence of an AIDS‑defining illness. In sub‑Saharan Africa, HIV prevalence is 4‑7 % and about 30 % of infected adults progress to AIDS within 10 years without treatment.
b: CD4 <200 cells/µL or AIDS‑defining condition = AIDS
HIV prevalence in East Africa ≈5 % (adult population)
≈30 % progress to AIDS within a decade without ART
Higher progression risk with malnutrition, TB co‑infection

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: The sole cause of AIDS is untreated HIV infection. Risk factors in East Africa include unprotected sex, contaminated needles, mother‑to‑child transmission, and limited access to testing and ART.
b: Unprotected heterosexual intercourse – most common route
Reuse of needles for injections or traditional practices
Vertical transmission during birth or breastfeeding
Late presentation for HIV testing
Co‑infection with TB or malaria accelerates CD4 loss

sections.p: HIV infects CD4+ T‑cells, macrophages and dendritic cells, integrating its RNA into host DNA. Ongoing replication depletes CD4 cells, impairs cytokine signaling and disables cell‑mediated immunity, allowing opportunistic pathogens to proliferate.
b: Reverse transcription of viral RNA → proviral DNA
Integration into host genome → chronic infection
Progressive CD4+ T‑cell depletion
Loss of Th1 cytokine response → opportunistic infection susceptibility
B‑cell dysfunction → hypergammaglobulinemia, poor vaccine response

sections.p: Patients may present with weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, persistent fever, lymphadenopathy, oral thrush, or AIDS‑defining cancers. In low‑resource settings, TB, cryptococcal meningitis and Kaposi sarcoma are frequent first clues.
b: Unexplained weight loss >10 % in 6 months (wasting)
Chronic watery diarrhoea (Cryptosporidium, CMV)
Persistent cough with night sweats (TB)
Oral thrush or esophageal candidiasis
Kaposi sarcoma lesions on skin or oral mucosa

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history should explore risk exposures, prior HIV testing, ART adherence, and symptoms of common opportunistic infections. Examination looks for lymphadenopathy, oral lesions, skin lesions, hepatosplenomegaly and neurologic deficits.
b: Ask about sexual partners, condom use, needle exposure, and childbirth history
Screen for fever, night sweats, diarrhoea, cough, skin lesions
Inspect oral cavity for thrush, ulcerations
Palpate cervical, axillary and inguinal nodes for size >1 cm
Auscultate lungs for crackles; percuss abdomen for hepatosplenomegaly

sections.p: Many infections mimic AIDS presentations; differentiate by CD4 count, epidemiology and specific signs.
b: TB vs. bacterial pneumonia – sputum smear, chest X‑ray pattern
Cryptosporidium diarrhoea vs. bacterial dysentery – stool microscopy
Kaposi sarcoma vs. bacillary angiomatosis – biopsy, response to antibiotics
Candidiasis vs. oral leukoplakia – white plaques that can be scraped
Malaria with splenomegaly vs. HIV‑related splenomegaly – rapid test, smear

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them

t.b: Immune status – <200 cells/µL confirms AIDS; 200‑499 indicates advanced HIV
Treatment monitoring – >100 000 copies/mL suggests poor control
Anemia, neutropenia, lymphopenia common; look for pancytopenia in advanced disease
Identify TB, Pneumocystis pneumonia (diffuse interstitial infiltrates) or Kaposi lesions
Detect Cryptosporidium oocysts; if unavailable, treat empirically for watery diarrhoea
Screen for cryptococcal meningitis – positive in CSF or serum warrants lumbar puncture

sections.p: WHO clinical staging (I–IV) and CD4 categories guide management. Stage IV or CD4 <200 cells/µL requires full opportunistic infection prophylaxis and ART initiation.
b: Stage I: Asymptomatic, CD4 ≥500
Stage II: Minor mucocutaneous manifestations, CD4 200‑499
Stage III: Moderate opportunistic infections, CD4 <200
Stage IV: AIDS‑defining illnesses, any CD4

sections.p: Co‑infection with TB, malaria, hepatitis B/C, and malnutrition worsen outcomes and may mask HIV‑related signs.
b: TB can cause false‑negative sputum if HIV‑induced paucibacillary disease
Malaria‑induced splenomegaly may be misattributed to HIV
Hepatitis B reactivation on ART – monitor liver enzymes
Severe anemia from chronic disease vs. zidovudine toxicity

sections.p: Start lifelong combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) as soon as diagnosis is confirmed, add prophylaxis for opportunistic infections, treat active infections, and provide psychosocial support.
b: Initiate cART (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir) regardless of CD4 when feasible
Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for Pneumocystis when CD4 <200
Isoniazid preventive therapy if no active TB and CD4 <350
Fluconazole for oral thrush; treat cryptococcal meningitis with amphotericin B + flucytosine if available
Counsel on adherence, nutrition, and safe sex

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening opportunistic infections and malignancies early; these require urgent referral or inpatient care.
b: Acute respiratory distress with diffuse infiltrates – suspect Pneumocystis pneumonia
Severe headache, neck stiffness – consider cryptococcal meningitis
Rapidly enlarging skin nodules – Kaposi sarcoma or bacillary angiomatosis
Persistent fever >4 weeks despite antibiotics – evaluate for TB or disseminated fungal infection
Neurologic decline – rule out toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma

sections.p: Pregnant women, children, and patients with renal/hepatic impairment need adapted regimens and closer monitoring.
b: Pregnant: use efavirenz‑based regimens after first trimester; avoid stavudine
Children: weight‑based dosing of pediatric fixed‑dose combos
Renal impairment: adjust tenofovir dose; monitor creatinine
Hepatitis B co‑infection: continue tenofovir‑based ART to suppress HBV

sections.p: With sustained ART, life expectancy approaches that of the general population. Regular CD4 and viral load monitoring, vaccination, and community education are essential.
b: CD4 and viral load every 3‑6 months after ART initiation
Vaccinate against pneumococcus, influenza, hepatitis B
Partner notification and testing to break transmission chains
Pre‑exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for high‑risk contacts
Nutrition support and treatment of co‑morbidities improve outcomes

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, false‑negative TB smears and variable CD4 assay quality can delay diagnosis.
b: Negative sputum does not rule out TB in HIV – consider GeneXpert or empirical therapy
CD4 counts may fluctuate; repeat if clinical picture discordant
Serum CrAg can be negative early; lumbar puncture still indicated with neurologic signs
Rapid HIV tests have window period – repeat after 4 weeks if recent exposure

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging skin lesions or ulcerations

faq.a: No; ART controls viral replication but does not eradicate HIV from the body.

faq.q: Why is CD4 count still used if viral load is available?
faq.a: CD4 reflects immune competence and guides prophylaxis, while viral load monitors treatment effectiveness.

faq.q: Is it safe to start ART during an active opportunistic infection?
faq.a: Yes, except for cryptococcal meningitis where ART is delayed 4‑6 weeks to avoid immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.

exam: A 32‑year‑old man presents with chronic diarrhoea and CD4 150 cells/µL. Which opportunistic infection is most likely and what is the first‑line treatment? — Cryptosporidium; start nitazoxanide if available, otherwise supportive rehydration and ART.

You have a patient with CD4 90 cells/µL and a new skin nodule. How do you differentiate Kaposi sarcoma from bacillary angiomatosis and why does it matter? — Biopsy; Kaposi responds to ART, bacillary angiomatosis requires macrolide antibiotics.

A pregnant woman with HIV is starting ART. Which regimen is preferred and why? — Tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir after first trimester; avoids efavirenz teratogenicity early and provides high barrier to resistance.

Explain why a negative sputum smear does not exclude TB in an AIDS patient and what alternative test you would order. — HIV reduces bacillary load; use GeneXpert MTB/RIF or start empirical therapy based on clinical picture.
What prophylactic medication is indicated for a patient with CD4 180 cells/µL and no active infection? — Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole daily for Pneumocystis prophylaxis.

A patient on ART develops new headaches and papilledema. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Cryptococcal meningitis; obtain CSF, start amphotericin B + flucytosine if available, then fluconazole consolidation.

Describe the WHO clinical stage IV criteria and its impact on management decisions. — Presence of any AIDS‑defining illness (e.g., Kaposi, PCP, TB meningitis); mandates full opportunistic infection prophylaxis and urgent ART optimization.

How does malnutrition influence HIV disease progression and what interventions are recommended? — Impairs immune recovery; provide nutritional supplementation, treat micronutrient deficiencies, and ensure ART adherence.

A patient with HIV and hepatitis B co‑infection is started on ART. Which drug component provides dual activity and why is it important? — Tenofovir; suppresses both HIV and HBV, preventing HBV flare when ART is stopped.

What are the red‑flag signs that require immediate referral for an AIDS patient presenting to a district hospital? — Acute respiratory failure, meningitis signs, severe dehydration, uncontrolled seizures, rapidly progressive Kaposi lesions.
